claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy with principal elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
A machine-learning-guided thermal treatment can induce beneficial surface segregation in the catalyst.
The thermal treatment can form a protective nanoscale oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer will enhance catalytic activity and durability under realistic low-temperature transient exhaust conditions.
The proposed improvement does not require an increase in platinum-group-metal content.
A computationally optimized annealing protocol will induce surface oxidation and atomic rearrangement.
Selective surface segregation will produce a stabilizing ultrathin protective oxide layer.
The oxide layer will mitigate deactivation caused by H2O and NO poisoning.
The oxide layer will mitigate sintering during thermal cycling.
The treated surface will retain active catalytic sites without additional platinum-group metals.
The treated catalyst will exhibit less activity loss than the untreated catalyst under the defined exhaust conditions.
The treated catalyst will exhibit better durability and more sustained performance through thermal-aging cycles than the untreated catalyst.
The expected effect is limited to simulated low-temperature transient exhaust operation with H2O and NO exposure and aging up to typical mileage limits.
The magnitude of performance improvement and the long-term durability of the oxide layer are uncertain.
